title: Relational vs NoSQL
description: Compare concrete data and consistency contracts across relational and NoSQL products, avoiding model stereotypes about schema, transactions, CAP, scaling, and performance.
notes:
## Comparing requirements before categories

Relational and NoSQL describe broad families of data organization and interfaces, not two products with one fixed capability list each. Relational designs emphasize relations, keys, and declarative operations. NoSQL is an umbrella commonly used for document, key-value, wide-column, graph, and related systems. Real implementations can overlap these descriptions and expose several access models.

The useful question is which implementation can preserve the required facts and operations under the intended workload. A label alone does not prove transaction support, lack of schema, horizontal scalability, or superior performance. Identify identity, relationship, validity, access, and failure requirements before selecting a database feature or comparing benchmark claims.

Consider a campus application with enrollment records, varied course descriptions, a catalog cache, and recommendation relationships. Those are different data and access needs, but they do not automatically require four different databases. A single established engine may support them adequately. Compare demonstrated limitations before introducing another operational system.

## Defining the facts and constraints

A relational enrollment model can represent one student-course occurrence through keys and association facts. Suitable foreign keys and uniqueness constraints can enforce selected relationships. These facilities are valuable when shared integrity and varied declarative queries matter, but the actual constraints must be defined and tested rather than inferred from the presence of tables.

A document model can group a course description with varied optional attributes. It still needs a contract for required identity, field types, and meaningful absence. Flexible shape does not mean no schema or no validation. Some products enforce write-time document rules, while applications also carry interpretation and evolution responsibilities.

Other models emphasize different access structures. Key-value access identifies an association by key; wide-column designs can organize keyed partitions for known queries; graph models expose relationship and path concepts. Each can be represented in several products with different guarantees. The subject matter alone, such as IoT or recommendations, does not uniquely determine the best engine.

## Distinguishing schema policy from model slogans

Schema-on-write commonly describes checking stored structure and rules before accepting a write. Schema-on-read emphasizes interpretation when data is consumed. Real systems often combine these ideas: a document may allow optional fields but require a stable identifier, while a relational table may contain a flexible JSON column with additional validation.

The absence of a rigid shape does not remove compatibility work. Changing duration from integer minutes to a sentence can break a document reader just as changing a relational column's meaning can break a report. A model comparison should ask how contracts evolve, how invalid states are rejected, and what older callers continue to expect.

Avoid using a large sparse relational table as the only possible relational design or a perfectly shaped single document as the only possible document design. Relations can use association tables and supported structured values. Documents can become oversized or duplicate shared facts. Compare credible designs for the same requirement rather than choosing deliberately weak examples.

## Comparing transactions precisely

An operation may require several row or document effects to become visible as one accepted unit. Determine the exact atomicity, isolation, and durability requirements. Some relational and non-relational products provide multi-record transactions under their supported rules. Others have narrower boundaries or different operational trade-offs. The family name is not enough evidence.

A ledger-like workflow often benefits from strong shared integrity and transaction guarantees, but that does not mean every relational configuration supplies the needed isolation automatically. Nor does it prove every document product lacks multi-document transactions. Verify the intended engine, version, storage, and application failure handling.

An external payment provider is another boundary. A local database commit does not automatically atomically include a remote charge merely because the database supports ACID. Such workflows require their own verified authority and coordination mechanisms. A database-model discussion must not imply that choosing a familiar engine solves every cross-system effect.

## Interpreting CAP without turning it into a slogan

The CAP result concerns defined consistency and availability properties under network partition in a distributed-system model. Its consistency notion is not simply every possible business constraint or the consistency letter in an ACID acronym. During a partition, an implementation cannot guarantee both the relevant single-copy behavior and a successful qualifying response for every required request under those assumptions.

This is not a universal instruction to choose any two letters forever, and it is not a classification that makes every relational engine consistent and every NoSQL engine available. Products offer different operation modes and failure behaviors. Identify what a caller actually requires when communication fails, and verify how the selected deployment handles that case.

BASE expands to Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency in common terminology. It describes a family of design ideas rather than a rigorous universal contract for all NoSQL products. Eventual convergence itself needs assumptions about updates, communication, and conflict handling. A label does not establish a precise freshness deadline for a user's next read.

## Evaluating distribution and scale

Relational modeling does not categorically prohibit horizontal distribution. Distributed SQL systems exist, while some NoSQL designs also face hot keys, cross-partition operations, or graph locality challenges. Distribution costs depend on required coordination and data placement rather than a universal rule that tables stay on one server and documents scale without effort.

An application with small traffic can be easier to operate on one established service. A high-volume workload may need carefully chosen partitions, indexes, replicas, or another supported design. The proposed change should follow measurements and requirements, including writes, reads, recovery, and operational expertise. More servers are not inherently simpler or faster.

Query language resemblance is also insufficient. Cassandra CQL looks SQL-like but has its own model, supported predicates, and distribution rules. Conversely, a product without a traditional SQL interface may still have useful indexes and transactional facilities. Inspect the actual feature contract rather than equating familiar syntax with identical behavior.

## Understanding duplication and read patterns

Normalized relations can reduce repeated authoritative facts. Embedded or precomputed representations can make a selected read convenient by storing an aggregate or projection together. Both designs have costs: assembling facts can require work, while copies need an explicit freshness and update policy. The number of visible joins is not a complete performance or correctness measure.

Suppose the authoritative enrollment count for a course is twelve, while a cached document says ten. That mismatch is a concrete consequence to investigate. It might reflect expected lag, a failed update, or an incorrect authority rule. Calling the cache NoSQL does not decide whether the mismatch is acceptable for the consumer.

The validation exercises use synthetic capability rows and snapshot counts. They test a stated requirement and detect absent or stale projection values in ordinary SQL. They do not benchmark a real vendor or verify native document-engine replication. This scope permits useful comparison practice without turning fixture labels into product recommendations.

## Defining evidence for a fair comparison

Choose representative original data, including repeated labels, missing optional values, boundary counts, and the relevant relationship cardinalities. Run equivalent operations with explicit output and ordering contracts. A faster query returning fewer required facts or weaker consistency is not an equivalent implementation of the task.

Record the engine, version, settings, data scale, and failure scope actually tested. MariaDB execution of a MySQL-oriented example is compatibility evidence, not exact provider verification. A local benchmark is not proof of production topology or authorization. Keep those claims distinct so reviewers can assess what the evidence supports.

A capability matrix should distinguish verified support from an untested assertion. The exercises use fictional store names for this reason. Passing a fixture query that selects a row marked verified does not itself verify that engine; it evaluates the modeled decision rule. Real selection still needs primary documentation and appropriate execution evidence.

## Choosing the smallest adequate design

Start with the existing system's contracts and the unmet requirement. Reuse its supported components where they fit, and compare alternatives only when there is a demonstrated need. Include migration, backup, monitoring, security, and recovery costs alongside query behavior. A fashionable model name is not sufficient justification for broadening an application's operational footprint.

Relational and NoSQL ideas are most useful as tools for expressing different facts and access patterns. Preserve exact meaning, trusted boundaries, and observable failure behavior across any comparison. That produces a defensible design choice without claiming that either broad family universally supplies every guarantee or wins every workload.

questions.question_text: What does the term 'NoSQL' most accurately refer to?
options: A single specific database product
An umbrella term for the family of non-relational data models: document, key-value, column-family, and graph
A query language that replaced SQL entirely
A model that only stores numeric data
questions.explanation: NoSQL is not one model but an umbrella covering multiple distinct non-relational paradigms, each with different trade-offs.

questions.question_text: What does 'schema-on-write' mean, as typically practiced by relational databases?
options: The schema is only checked when data is read
The table structure is defined and enforced before data is inserted
There is no schema at all
Schema changes never require a migration
questions.explanation: Schema-on-write means the structure must be defined and validated at write/insert time, contrasting with schema-on-read used by many NoSQL document stores.

questions.question_text: What does the BASE consistency model (often associated with distributed NoSQL systems) stand for?
options: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Binary Atomic Strict Execution
Backup Available, Synchronized, Encrypted
Batch Access, Single Endpoint
questions.explanation: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency — a deliberate trade favoring availability over the strict guarantees of ACID.

questions.question_text: Under the CAP model, what tension arises during a network partition?
options: The specified consistency and availability guarantees cannot both be maintained for all required requests under the theorem assumptions
Cost and Performance
Schema and Storage
Security and Speed
questions.explanation: CAP consistency is not simply every business rule or ACID consistency, and the result is not a choose-any-two-forever slogan.

questions.question_text: Does the relational model categorically forbid horizontal distribution?
options: Because SQL cannot run on multiple servers under any circumstances
No; actual coordination, partitioning, and product capabilities determine distribution behavior
Because relational databases are always faster on a single machine regardless of workload
Because horizontal scaling was not invented until after SQL
questions.explanation: Distributed SQL implementations exist; model labels do not fix topology.

questions.question_text: What should guide a choice for a ledger-like workflow requiring shared integrity and atomic updates?
options: Petabyte-scale IoT sensor telemetry ingestion
Verified transaction, integrity, access, and operational guarantees for the actual workflow
A simple session cache needing sub-millisecond key lookups
A social network requiring deep friend-of-friend traversal
questions.explanation: Do not assume every relational configuration supplies the needed behavior or every NoSQL product lacks it.

questions.question_text: Does Cassandra CQL's SQL-like appearance make its behavior identical to a relational database?
options: Yes, CQL syntax guarantees identical consistency and query capabilities to SQL
No; its supported model, access patterns, and operation guarantees need their own review
Yes, because CQL supports arbitrary multi-table joins just like SQL
No, because CQL cannot filter data at all
questions.explanation: Syntax resemblance does not establish semantic or operational equivalence.

questions.question_text: Does IoT telemetry alone prove a wide-column engine is the best choice?
options: No; evaluate the actual keys, queries, consistency, volume, and operational requirements
Pure hierarchical model
Object-oriented model
Graph model
questions.explanation: A common use case is not a universal product recommendation.

questions.question_text: Does flexible document structure imply no possible write validation?
options: Yes; all documents are unvalidated
No
Only relational JSON can have rules
Only if a key is absent
questions.explanation: Real systems can combine optional fields with enforced requirements.

questions.question_text: What does a verified capability matrix need to distinguish?
options: Only product logos
Only query indentation
Actual support evidence from an untested assertion
Only the number of columns in a demo
questions.explanation: A claimed feature is not the same as verified support.

questions.question_text: A workflow needs atomic multi-record updates. What should selection inspect?
options: Only whether the product is called NoSQL
Only whether its syntax uses SELECT
The exact supported transaction boundary and failure behavior
Only whether a demo read is fast
questions.explanation: Capabilities depend on product, configuration, and operation.

questions.question_text: An authoritative count is 12 but a snapshot says 10. What needs evaluation?
options: Only the model label
Only the database file name
Only the visible table width
Freshness policy and the cause of the mismatch
questions.explanation: A concrete inconsistency needs a contract and diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Two implementations differ in required returned facts. Is a latency comparison automatically equivalent?
options: No
Yes; any faster response wins
Only if both use SQL
Only if the sample is small
questions.explanation: Performance must be compared for the same result and guarantees.

questions.question_text: A document duration changes from minutes to a sentence. What still needs review?
options: Nothing because documents have no schema
Reader compatibility and value meaning
Only the document ID length
Only the number of servers
questions.explanation: Flexible representation does not remove data contracts.

questions.question_text: A database commits an order. What does that alone not prove about an external charge?
options: That local work had a transaction
That a source record can exist
That the remote provider effect participated atomically
That a workflow has requirements
questions.explanation: Cross-system authority and coordination are separate boundaries.

questions.question_text: A small service fits its existing database. What cost should justify adding another engine?
options: Only a fashionable model name
Only a larger benchmark screenshot
Only a desire for more servers
A demonstrated unmet requirement weighed against operational complexity
questions.explanation: Use the smallest adequate verified design.

questions.question_text: A store is marked unverified despite claimed joins and transactions. Should the fixture treat it as a verified candidate?
options: No
Yes; claims are enough
Only if its name sounds relational
Only if it has a fast connection
questions.explanation: The decision rule requires evidence status as well as capability flags.

questions.question_text: A cache row exists but its count is NULL. Is that the same as no cache row?
options: Yes; every missing value has one cause
No
Only if the source count is zero
Only if IDs match
questions.explanation: A missing projection and an unknown projection value are distinct states.

questions.question_text: A native product has an SQL-like language. What should not be inferred?
options: That its grammar may be documented
That it supports some statements
Identical model, query, and consistency semantics
That its actual features can be tested
questions.explanation: Familiar spelling does not guarantee equivalence.

questions.question_text: A MariaDB fixture passes. What remains outside that evidence?
options: The observed SQL output
The fixture values used
The recorded local engine
Exact MySQL/provider and distributed failure behavior
questions.explanation: Verification scope follows the actual environment.

coding_problems.title: Filter fictional stores by verified requirements
coding_problems.task: Return store_name for fictional capability_matrix rows where supports_atomic_updates=1, supports_joins=1, and verified=1. Order by store_name. This evaluates a supplied requirement matrix, not actual vendor features or a product recommendation.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE capability_matrix (store_name VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY, supports_atomic_updates INT NOT NULL CHECK(supports_atomic_updates IN (0,1)), supports_joins INT NOT NULL CHECK(supports_joins IN (0,1)), verified INT NOT NULL CHECK(verified IN (0,1)));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO capability_matrix VALUES ('Store A',1,1,1),('Store B',1,0,1),('Store C',1,1,0),('Store D',0,1,1);
constraints: Flags express supplied fixture facts only
Every required flag must be true
edge_cases: Claimed but unverified support is excluded
Missing one required capability excludes the row
No qualifying store returns no rows
hints: Combine all three requirements with AND
Do not infer features from a store name
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT store_name FROM capability_matrix WHERE supports_atomic_updates=1 AND supports_joins=1 AND verified=1 ORDER BY store_name;
coding_problems.explanation: The explicit conjunction evaluates the stated evidence rule without making claims about real products.

coding_problems.title: Expose missing and stale precomputed counts
coding_problems.task: For every authoritative_counts row, return course_id, enrollment_count, cached_count, state. State is missing when no snapshot exists, unknown when a snapshot row has NULL cached_count, current when counts match, and stale otherwise. Order by course_id. Snapshot data is a relational teaching mirror, not a native document-store connection.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE authoritative_counts (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, enrollment_count INT NOT NULL CHECK(enrollment_count>=0));
CREATE TABLE snapshots (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, cached_count INT NULL CHECK(cached_count>=0));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO authoritative_counts VALUES (1,12),(2,0),(3,5),(4,8); INSERT INTO snapshots VALUES (1,10),(2,0),(4,NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
course_id	enrollment_count	cached_count	state
1	12	10	stale
2	0	0	current
3	5	NULL	missing
4	8	NULL	unknown
constraints: One authoritative and at most one snapshot row per course
NULL snapshot count is unrecorded, not zero
Only authoritative course population is requested
edge_cases: Missing row differs from a NULL-valued existing row
Other snapshot IDs do not create authoritative facts
hints: Preserve source rows with a left join
Test snapshot identity before testing its nullable count
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT a.course_id,a.enrollment_count,s.cached_count,CASE WHEN s.course_id IS NULL THEN 'missing' WHEN s.cached_count IS NULL THEN 'unknown' WHEN s.cached_count=a.enrollment_count THEN 'current' ELSE 'stale' END AS state FROM authoritative_counts a LEFT JOIN snapshots s ON s.course_id=a.course_id ORDER BY a.course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The source-preserving join and ordered CASE retain distinct absence and mismatch states. They detect a modeled discrepancy without deciding whether a real freshness policy permits it.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO authoritative_counts VALUES (1,0); INSERT INTO snapshots VALUES (1,NULL);
validation_cases.expected:
course_id	enrollment_count	cached_count	state
1	0	NULL	unknown

original_questions.question_text: What does the term 'NoSQL' most accurately refer to?
options: A single specific database product
An umbrella term for the family of non-relational data models: document, key-value, column-family, and graph
A query language that replaced SQL entirely
A model that only stores numeric data
original_questions.explanation: NoSQL is not one model but an umbrella covering multiple distinct non-relational paradigms, each with different trade-offs.

original_questions.question_text: What does 'schema-on-write' mean, as typically practiced by relational databases?
options: The schema is only checked when data is read
The table structure is defined and enforced before data is inserted
There is no schema at all
Schema changes never require a migration
original_questions.explanation: Schema-on-write means the structure must be defined and validated at write/insert time, contrasting with schema-on-read used by many NoSQL document stores.

original_questions.question_text: What does the BASE consistency model (often associated with distributed NoSQL systems) stand for?
options: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Binary Atomic Strict Execution
Backup Available, Synchronized, Encrypted
Batch Access, Single Endpoint
original_questions.explanation: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency — a deliberate trade favoring availability over the strict guarantees of ACID.

original_questions.question_text: According to the CAP theorem, what must a distributed system choose between when a network partition occurs?
options: Consistency and Availability
Cost and Performance
Schema and Storage
Security and Speed
original_questions.explanation: CAP theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency (all nodes see the same data) and Availability (every request gets a response) — it cannot guarantee both.

original_questions.question_text: Why do relational databases traditionally scale vertically rather than horizontally?
options: Because SQL cannot run on multiple servers under any circumstances
Because joins and ACID transactions across a normalized schema are hard to distribute correctly across many independent nodes
Because relational databases are always faster on a single machine regardless of workload
Because horizontal scaling was not invented until after SQL
original_questions.explanation: Maintaining ACID guarantees and efficient joins across a normalized schema is difficult to distribute cleanly, which historically pushed relational systems toward scaling up rather than out.

original_questions.question_text: Which of the following is a scenario where a relational database is generally the better choice over NoSQL alternatives?
options: Petabyte-scale IoT sensor telemetry ingestion
A banking ledger requiring strong ACID consistency and complex ad-hoc joins
A simple session cache needing sub-millisecond key lookups
A social network requiring deep friend-of-friend traversal
original_questions.explanation: Banking ledgers need strong consistency and support complex evolving queries across normalized data, which plays to the relational model's strengths.

original_questions.question_text: Does a NoSQL system like Cassandra's CQL using SQL-like syntax mean it behaves like a relational database?
options: Yes, CQL syntax guarantees identical consistency and query capabilities to SQL
No — the underlying data model (column-family) and consistency guarantees (tunable, often eventual) still differ fundamentally from a relational database, regardless of syntax similarity
Yes, because CQL supports arbitrary multi-table joins just like SQL
No, because CQL cannot filter data at all
original_questions.explanation: Syntax resemblance does not change the underlying architecture; Cassandra's column-family model and tunable/eventual consistency remain fundamentally different from relational ACID semantics.

original_questions.question_text: Which database model would be the best fit for an application whose primary need is massive write throughput for time-series IoT sensor data?
options: Column-family model
Pure hierarchical model
Object-oriented model
Graph model
original_questions.explanation: Column-family stores like Cassandra are specifically optimized for very high write throughput and horizontal scale, making them well suited to time-series/IoT telemetry.

diagrams.caption: Compare contracts rather than model stereotypes
diagrams.description: The questions apply to actual product versions and operations. A category label is not evidence that a required capability exists or a trade-off is acceptable.
rows: Defined and enforced keys or schema rules
Actual operation boundary and failure policy
Partitioning and coordination under the workload
Source authority and projection lag policy
A fast cache must be current
